questions.stem: What does a security group do in an Amazon VPC?

options.text: Acts as a virtual firewall controlling traffic to and from instances
options.rationale: Security groups control inbound and outbound traffic for the resources they are attached to.

options.text: Encrypts data stored on Amazon EBS volumes
options.rationale: Encryption at rest is a storage feature, not a security group function.

options.text: Gives a set of IAM users the same permissions
options.rationale: That is an IAM group.

options.text: Scans instances for malware and vulnerabilities
options.rationale: Vulnerability scanning is done by Amazon Inspector.

questions.explanation: Security groups work at the instance (network interface) level; network ACLs work at the subnet level.

questions.stem: Which statement about security groups and network ACLs is correct?

options.text: Security groups are stateless; network ACLs are stateful
options.rationale: This reverses the two.

options.text: Security groups are stateful; network ACLs are stateless
options.rationale: Return traffic is automatically allowed by a security group, but a network ACL evaluates each direction separately.

options.text: Both are applied at the subnet level
options.rationale: Security groups apply to instances; network ACLs apply to subnets.

options.text: Network ACLs cannot contain deny rules
options.rationale: Network ACLs support both allow and deny rules.

questions.explanation: Security groups support allow rules only and are stateful. Network ACLs support allow and deny rules and are stateless.

questions.stem: At which level does a network ACL control traffic in an Amazon VPC?

options.rationale: Instance-level control is done with security groups.
Network ACLs belong to a VPC and apply to subnets, not whole Regions.
A network ACL allows or denies traffic in and out of a subnet.
Network ACLs are not account-wide controls.

questions.explanation: Network ACLs are an optional layer of security at the subnet level, in addition to security groups.

questions.stem: Which service protects web applications from common exploits such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting?

options.rationale: Shield focuses on DDoS protection.
GuardDuty detects threats from account and network activity.
Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities.
AWS WAF is a web application firewall that filters HTTP and HTTPS requests based on rules.

questions.explanation: AWS WAF protects at the application layer with rules for common attack patterns; Shield protects against DDoS.

questions.stem: Where can a company find and buy third-party security software, such as firewalls and endpoint protection, that runs on AWS?

options.rationale: AWS Marketplace is a catalog of third-party software, including security products.
Artifact provides compliance reports.
Security Hub aggregates findings; it is not a software store.
Trusted Advisor checks your account against best practices.

questions.explanation: AWS Marketplace offers third-party security solutions from AWS Partners that integrate with AWS services.

questions.stem: Which service can check an AWS account for security issues such as security groups with unrestricted ports or a root user without MFA?

options.rationale: Artifact provides compliance reports.
Trusted Advisor includes security checks such as open ports and root account MFA.
Inspector scans workloads for software vulnerabilities, not account settings like root MFA.
Shield protects against DDoS attacks.

questions.explanation: Trusted Advisor inspects your environment and recommends improvements in categories including cost optimization, performance, resilience, security, operational excellence and service limits.

questions.stem: Where can a customer find articles answering common AWS questions, written by AWS Support engineers?

options.rationale: Artifact provides compliance reports.
Marketplace is a software catalog.
The Knowledge Center, part of AWS re:Post, answers frequently asked questions from AWS customers.
Cost Explorer analyzes spending.

questions.explanation: AWS security information is found in the Knowledge Center, the AWS security website (aws.amazon.com/security) and the AWS Security Blog.

questions.stem: Where would a customer read posts by AWS security experts about new security features and best practices?

options.rationale: Artifact provides compliance reports and agreements.
Cost Explorer analyzes spending.
AWS Config records resource configurations.
The AWS Security Blog publishes security guidance, announcements and how-to posts.

questions.explanation: The AWS Security Blog is one of the main sources of security information, along with the Knowledge Center and the AWS security website.

questions.stem: By default, which traffic does a newly created security group allow?

options.text: All outbound traffic, and no inbound traffic
options.rationale: A new security group has no inbound rules and an outbound rule that allows all traffic.

options.text: All inbound and all outbound traffic
options.rationale: Inbound traffic is denied until you add rules.

options.text: No inbound and no outbound traffic
options.rationale: Outbound traffic is allowed by default.

options.text: Inbound web traffic on port 80 alone
options.rationale: No inbound rules exist by default.

questions.explanation: Security groups deny inbound traffic unless a rule allows it, which is why you add rules for the ports your application needs.

questions.stem: Which TWO can be used to control network traffic in an Amazon VPC? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: Cost Explorer analyzes spending.
Network ACLs filter traffic for subnets.
Artifact provides compliance reports.
Security groups filter traffic for instances and other resources.
Password policies apply to IAM user sign-in, not network traffic.

questions.explanation: Security groups and network ACLs are the two VPC traffic controls; using both adds defense in depth.
